claims.text: Brittle behavior in compositionally complex high-entropy alloys emerges from stress- and temperature-induced short-range ordering and nanoscale solute segregation at grain boundaries.
Brittle behavior does not arise from bulk intermetallic precipitation or grain coarsening under the proposed conditions.
Localized chemical partitioning weakens intergranular cohesion.
Weakened intergranular cohesion leads to premature crack initiation under service loads.
The initial alloy is single phase and has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The initial alloy contains no large-scale precipitates.
Elevated temperature and applied stress enhance elemental mobility.
Enhanced mobility causes particular solute species to segregate subtly to grain boundaries.
The segregated grain-boundary zones exhibit short-range order.
Short-range-ordered, chemically inhomogeneous grain-boundary zones reduce grain-boundary cohesive strength.
The alloy can undergo brittle fracture while retaining its overall single-phase character.
Thermally aged and mechanically loaded specimens will show detectable nanoscale grain-boundary segregation relative to the as-processed baseline.
Thermally aged and mechanically loaded specimens will have lower fracture toughness than the as-processed baseline.
The predicted toughness decrease will occur without large-scale intermetallic formation or significant grain coarsening.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate when temperatures approach 650–750 °C and sustained mechanical loading is applied for extended durations.
The proposed mechanism may not be significant at lower temperatures or very high strain rates.
The proposed mechanism may not dominate in environments where oxidation or another degradation mechanism prevails.
